There are three hundred pages of calculations, drawings, failed tests and curses. In the last twenty pages, after the night of the two lights, the handwriting changes. It becomes small, tight and obsessed. Every night for four months the old man tried to turn the Machine on again, always at a quarter past eleven. He never did it. The last page, written a few days before he died, has only one line: *perhaps it is not for me to do.*
Lo leggete a turno, fino all'alba, alla.short: You read it in turns until dawn. After the two lights the hand turns small and obsessive: every night for four months, at a quarter past eleven, he tried to turn the Machine on again. The last page says only: *perhaps it is not for me to do.*

Ricopiate a mano le pagine più important.easy: You copy by hand the most important pages, about the two lights and the months after, and you take them to Hester Maas. She puts them in the Register without reading them, between a birth certificate and a receipt. "Someone after me will read them," she says. "Someone who will have more time than me."
Ricopiate a mano le pagine più important.short: You copy the key pages for Hester Maas, who slips them unread into the Register. "Someone after me will read them. Someone with more time."

La pietra è nella torbiera, e nessuno de.easy: The stone is in the bog, and nobody in the family has it now. But someone must take care of the Machine.
La pietra è nella torbiera, e nessuno de.short: The stone is in the bog. But someone must keep the Machine.

La custodia della torre, del quaderno e.easy: The tower, the notebook and the Machine go to the person who had the stone for the longest time, or to the person the family chooses. Next to the notebook there is something else that your father left on the table, near his pen. It is his silver pocket watch, the one from his waistcoat. It is new and shiny, with the crest of the estate. It has stopped at a quarter past eleven. You wind it up, and it starts again.
La custodia della torre, del quaderno e.short: The Machine goes to whoever kept the stone longest, or whom the family chooses. Beside the notebook lies your father's own watch, new and shiny, stopped at a quarter past eleven. You wind it, and it runs.

Da quel giorno chi ha la Macchina lo por.easy: From that day, the person who has the Machine always carries the watch. Nobody in the family thinks this is strange. Only Hester Maas goes pale when she sees it. She goes home to look in the drawer where she keeps the Register.
Da quel giorno chi ha la Macchina lo por.short: Whoever keeps the Machine now carries the watch. Only Hester Maas, seeing it, turns pale and hurries home to check her drawer.

Sono vecchia, e la mano non mi aiuta più.easy: I am old, and my hand does not help me any more. This is the last page I will write. I leave the Register to my son Joost. He studied medicine in the city, and now he is coming back to {0} as the village doctor. He laughs at my cold hands. He has studied, and people who have studied do not count. They measure.
Sono vecchia, e la mano non mi aiuta più.short: I am old; this is my last page. I leave the Register to my son Joost, the new village doctor. He laughs at my cold hands. He has studied: he does not count, he measures.

Gli eredi della tenuta sono invecchiati,.easy: The heirs of the estate are old now, like me. Some of them have died of old age, in their beds, with warm hands. I touched them myself. The Machine is still in the tower, silent. Their children grew up in {0}, and they do not know what {1} was like before.
Gli eredi della tenuta sono invecchiati,.short: The heirs of the estate have grown old. Some died in their beds, hands warm: I checked. The Machine stands silent. Their children do not know what {0} was before.

La pietra è tornata nella torbiera. Ques.easy: The stone is back in the bog. This winter the place where the light was did not freeze, not even on the coldest nights.
La pietra è tornata nella torbiera. Ques.short: The stone is back in the bog. This winter the place of the light never froze.

La pietra è ancora alla tenuta, sulla me.easy: The stone is still at the estate, on the shelf in the laboratory. The family drinks a lot of water. They buy it in the city.
La pietra è ancora alla tenuta, sulla me.short: The stone is still on the laboratory shelf. The family drinks a lot of water, bought in the city.

I nomi nel Registro, quelli con le mani.easy: In the Register there are one hundred and fourteen names with cold hands. The village has three hundred and twenty people. I do not tell anyone. Who could I tell?
I nomi nel Registro, quelli con le mani.short: One hundred and fourteen cold hands in the Register, out of three hundred and twenty villagers. Who would I tell?

Illustre collega, vi scrivo da {0}, un p.easy: Dear colleague, I am writing to you from {0}, a village of peat-cutters half a day away by train. I came here for the object I told you about: the so-called "stone of the light". I am coming back with nothing. A member of the family of the estate, {1}, bought it at the auction, for a price the museum would never accept. But I will describe it to you anyway, so that we have a record.
Illustre collega, vi scrivo da {0}, un p.short: Dear colleague, I return from {0} empty-handed: the "stone of the light" went to {1}, of the estate, for a sum the museum would never approve. For the record, a description.

Pietra nera, liscia, grande come una pag.easy: A black stone, smooth, as big as a loaf of bread, and strangely heavy. Its temperature never changes, and it is warmer than the air around it: you can feel the heat through the sack. You cannot see any crystals or any cracks. It is not any kind of meteorite I know. The peat-cutter who found it, a man called Tammer, held it like a living thing.
Pietra nera, liscia, grande come una pag.short: Black, smooth, oddly heavy, always warm. No crystals, no cracks: no meteorite I know of. The peat-cutter who found it held it like a living thing.

Aggiungo un'impressione personale, di cu.easy: I add a personal feeling, but please do not talk about it to the board. {0} is the quietest village I have ever seen. At the auction nobody raised their voice. Nobody tried to get a lower price. When the auctioneer hit the table with his hammer, the whole crowd clapped at the same moment, and stopped at the same moment. At the inn I asked for beer, but they gave me water. The innkeeper smiled and said that "it is better for everyone".
Aggiungo un'impressione personale, di cu.short: Privately: {0} is the quietest village I have known. The crowd clapped all at once and stopped all at once. I asked for beer and was served water: "better for everyone", smiled the innkeeper.

Ho lasciato il mio biglietto da visita a.easy: I left my card with the family. I plan to come back. Yours most faithfully, J. Ostrander.
Ho lasciato il mio biglietto da visita a.short: I left my card with the family. I shall return. J. Ostrander.

Alla Traveling Caravan, davanti al carro.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, in front of the cart that sells tickets for the coach to the city, there is Harm Visser, the miller. He has a bundle in his hand and looks like he has not slept for weeks. He wants to leave, he says, but he is not brave enough to buy the ticket. Since the winter, his wife Grietje is different. She sings while she works, and before she always sang out of tune. She does not fight with his mother any more, and before she hated her. Every evening she kisses him on the forehead. She never did that before, not even when they were just married. She is perfect. He is more afraid of her than he has ever been of anything.
Alla Traveling Caravan, davanti al carro.short: Harm Visser the miller stands by the coach-ticket cart with a bundle, not daring to buy. Since winter his wife Grietje sings in tune, loves her mother-in-law, kisses him goodnight. She is perfect, and he has never been so afraid.

\"Ditemi che sono pazzo\", ti chiede. \".easy: "Tell me that I am mad," he asks you. "You people at the estate have studied. Tell me, and I will go home."
\"Ditemi che sono pazzo\", ti chiede. \".short: "Tell me I am mad. You have studied. Tell me, and I will go home."

Harm ti ringrazia, sollevato, come un ma.easy: Harm thanks you. He is relieved, like a sick man when the doctor tells him it is nothing. He goes home with his bundle under his arm. The next month you see him at the market. His shirt is ironed, his hands are clean, and he has a calm smile. He nods to you, kindly. He does not thank you any more.
Harm ti ringrazia, sollevato, come un ma.short: Harm goes home relieved. A month later, at the market, he has an ironed shirt, clean hands and a calm smile. He nods to you kindly. He no longer thanks you.

Gli compri il biglietto e lo accompagni.easy: You buy his ticket and walk with him to the coach. Harm sits at the back, holding his bundle tight, and does not look back. Grietje does not come to say goodbye. But the next day she comes to the estate with a cake, to thank the family "for helping poor Harm, who was not well". The cake is perfect.
Gli compri il biglietto e lo accompagni.short: Harm leaves on the coach without looking back. Next day Grietje brings the estate a cake, "for helping poor Harm, who was not well". The cake is perfect.

Harm ci pensa. La notte di San Nicola, d.easy: Harm thinks. On Saint Nicholas' night, he says, Grietje went out to get water from the canal, because the well was frozen. She came back an hour later, dry, without the bucket. She said the canal was beautiful at night, and she was not cold. Then she went to bed and slept very quietly. That night he cried, and he did not know why.
Harm ci pensa. La notte di San Nicola, d.short: On Saint Nicholas' night Grietje went to the canal for water. She came back an hour later, dry, without the bucket, saying it was beautiful there. That night Harm cried without knowing why.

Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has opened a council decision on the table. It is signed and stamped. It says the tower of the estate is "unsafe" and must be knocked down before the end of the year, paid for by the town, to keep people safe. Lambert reads it out in his calm voice. He has not had bandages on his hands for years. He offers to do the job himself, with his men, for free. "Then you will not have to think about it," he says. "Then nobody will have to think about it."
Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.short: Lambert reads out a council resolution: the estate's tower is "unsafe" and must come down this year. He offers to do it himself, free. "Then nobody need think about it any more."

Lambert non insiste. Riarrotola la delib.easy: Lambert does not insist. He rolls up the paper carefully, ties it with string and puts it in the drawer. The council will not talk about it again. But in the evening, from the window of the estate, you see Lambert standing in the road. He looks at the tower for an hour without moving, the way you look at an old enemy, or an old friend.
Lambert non insiste. Riarrotola la delib.short: Lambert puts the resolution away without a word. But that evening he stands in the road for an hour, motionless, looking at the tower like an old enemy, or an old friend.

Lambert accetta, con la stessa calma. I.easy: Lambert says yes, just as calmly. His men work for a month: iron chains around the walls, new stairs, oak beams. They work very well, better than anyone has ever worked in {0}. But they never go above the stairs. They say the room at the top is not their business.
Lambert accetta, con la stessa calma. I.short: Lambert's men shore up the tower beautifully in a month. But they never go above the stairs. The room at the top, they say, is not their concern.

Lambert ti mostra la prima pagina della.easy: Lambert shows you the first page of the decision. Three councillors signed the proposal: Mayor Wessel, the clerk and a new councillor. The whole village voted for him this year. The new councillor is Fokke Tammer. Twenty years ago he could not write his name. Now his signature is elegant and even, like a notary's.
Lambert ti mostra la prima pagina della.short: The resolution is signed by the mayor, the clerk and a new councillor elected unanimously: Fokke Tammer. Twenty years ago he could not write his name. His signature is a notary's.

Al Town Hall il sindaco Aldert Wessel ti.easy: At the Town Hall, Mayor Aldert Wessel meets you with his bandaged foot on a stool. He holds a handkerchief and wipes his forehead every two minutes. He is a big, red, sweaty man who talks too much and laughs at his own jokes. In the village they call him "the fish" because his hands are always wet. He knows it, and he laughs about it. He has an offer: the town wants to buy the tower of the estate, "to make a water tank", and will pay well. He says your father owed him money. A lot of money. And that tower, at night, with its blue flashes, frightened his wife.
Al Town Hall il sindaco Aldert Wessel ti.short: Mayor Wessel, big, red and sweaty, his gouty foot on a stool, offers to buy the tower "for a water tank". Your father owed him money, he says. And its blue flashes frightened his wife.

Il sindaco conta il denaro due volte, co.easy: The mayor counts the money twice with his sweaty fingers and signs the receipt with a big flourish. Then he gives you a cigar and, laughing, tells you three rude jokes about Pastor Kalf. They are terrible. You leave the Town Hall with a headache and a strange feeling of affection for this loud man.
Il sindaco conta il denaro due volte, co.short: The mayor counts the money twice, signs with a flourish and tells three dreadful jokes about the pastor. You leave with a headache and a strange fondness for him.

Il sindaco si offende, diventa più rosso.easy: The mayor is offended. His face gets redder and he raises his voice. He says the estate is not above the law, and the council has ways to get what it wants. Then, as always, he calms down, wipes his forehead and says sorry. It is the gout, he says, that makes him nervous. He limps with you to the door and shakes your hand. His hand is wet and warm.
Il sindaco si offende, diventa più rosso.short: The mayor shouts that the estate is not above the law, then calms down and blames his gout. At the door he shakes your hand. It is damp and warm.

Il sindaco smette di ridere. Quella nott.easy: The mayor stops laughing. That night, he says, his foot hurt and he could not sleep. From the window he saw everything: the light on the tower and the light on the bog, at the same moment, like two lanterns sending signals to each other. He was afraid. He did not tell anyone, because a mayor is never afraid. "But you are the family," he says. "You must know what you have in your house."
Il sindaco smette di ridere. Quella nott.short: The mayor stops laughing. That night he saw both lights at once, like two lanterns signalling. He was afraid, and told nobody. "But you are the family. You must know what is in your house."

Al Park, la mattina di Pasqua, c'è una f.easy: At the Park, on Easter morning, a crowd in white shirts stands by the pond. It is a new tradition. It started two years ago, but nobody decided it. People who want to start the year "clean" walk into the water up to their waist and come out in silence. The water there comes straight from the bog. Pastor Kalf is not there: he says it is a pagan custom. Mayor Wessel is there, at the front, holding hands with the people who are afraid. Someone reaches out a hand to you. They smile.
Al Park, la mattina di Pasqua, c'è una f.short: On Easter morning a crowd in white wades waist-deep into the pond, fed by the bog, to begin the year "clean". The pastor stays away; the mayor holds the frightened by the hand. Someone smiles and reaches out to you.

L'acqua è gelida, poi non più. Resti lì,.easy: The water is ice cold, and then it is not. You stand there with the water up to your waist and a stranger's hand in yours. For a long moment nobody breathes. When you come out, people hug you, one after the other. You go home feeling light, with no worries. Not even one.
L'acqua è gelida, poi non più. Resti lì,.short: The water is icy, then not. For a long moment nobody breathes. Coming out, you are embraced by everyone, and go home without a single care.

Resti sulla riva con il taccuino. Entran.easy: You stay on the bank with your notebook. Forty-two people go in. Forty-two come out. But three of them were coughing when they went in, and when they come out they are not coughing. One was limping, and now walks straight. A girl was crying, and now she is smiling. You write down the names. When you look up, the people who came out of the water are standing in a line, looking at you kindly.
Resti sulla riva con il taccuino. Entran.short: Forty-two go in, forty-two come out. But the coughs, a limp, a girl's tears are gone. You note the names. When you look up, they stand in a row, watching you kindly.

Riprendo il Registro di mia madre, per r.easy: I continue my mother's Register, out of respect and out of habit, and with one plan: I will only write things that can be measured. My mother was a clever woman and a very good midwife. But in her last years she counted cold hands the way other people count prayers. I studied in the city. In medicine, cold hands are called bad circulation.
Riprendo il Registro di mia madre, per r.short: I take up my mother's Register, and will write only what can be measured. In her last years she counted cold hands like rosary beads. In medicine, cold hands are poor circulation.

Il paese non è più quello in cui sono na.easy: The village is not the one where I was born. The wooden houses are now brick houses, with wooden beams and tiled roofs. The dyke is higher, the mill is new, the church is bigger. Three years in a row, the council has given the village the prize for the tidiest village in the province. There are no thieves, no debts and no fights at the inn, because nobody goes to the inn any more. The church choir is the best in the diocese.
Il paese non è più quello in cui sono na.short: The village is not the one I was born in: brick houses, a higher dyke, a new mill, three years the tidiest village in the province. No thefts, no debts, no brawls: nobody goes to the inn. The choir is the best in the diocese.

Qualche famiglia, negli anni, se n'è and.easy: Over the years some families have left: the Mulders, the De Graafs, the widow Brink, about twelve in all. They said they were not happy here any more. Their houses are still empty, and nobody buys them. The roofs are falling in, the windows are broken, and grass grows on the doorsteps. In such a tidy village, these ruins look wrong. The mayor has promised to knock them down.
Qualche famiglia, negli anni, se n'è and.short: A dozen families have left over the years, saying they no longer felt at home. Their empty houses are falling down, out of place in so tidy a village. The mayor will have them demolished.

Alla tenuta vivono ora i nipoti del vecc.easy: Now the old man's grandchildren live at the estate. The tower is open. The Machine is still there, under a sheet, and nobody knows how to make it work.
Alla tenuta vivono ora i nipoti del vecc.short: The old man's grandchildren live at the estate now. The Machine waits under a sheet. Nobody can make it work.

La prima settimana dell'anno arriva alla.easy: In the first week of the year a young man from the council comes to the estate. He has a neat beard and his hands are in his pockets. It is Bram Wessel, the mayor's son. He has an offer. The houses of the families who left are for sale, very cheap. The council would like the estate to buy them, because they are "people from here", and not some stranger. He says the council would be happy to help repair them.
La prima settimana dell'anno arriva alla.short: Bram Wessel, the mayor's son, hands in pockets, offers the estate the empty houses for next to nothing: better "people from here" than outsiders. The council would gladly help do them up.

Mentre parla, chiedi notizie di sua madr.easy: While he talks, you ask about his mother, Mrs Wessel, who went to the city many years ago. Bram smiles. She is still at her sister's, she is very well, and she writes every week. She has never come back. He does not think this is strange.
Mentre parla, chiedi notizie di sua madr.short: You ask after his mother, gone to the city years ago. Still at her sister's, Bram smiles, writing every week. She has never come back. He finds nothing strange in it.

Firmate, pagate pochissimo, e la settima.easy: You sign and pay very little. The next week a group of workers from the village is already working: new roofs, new windows, white walls. They work without pay, smiling. When you ask why, they say it is a pleasure to help their neighbours.
Firmate, pagate pochissimo, e la settima.short: You buy them cheaply, and the next week village workmen are rebuilding them, unpaid and smiling. "It is a pleasure to help one's neighbours."

Scrivete a tutte le famiglie partite, ag.easy: You write to all the families who left, at the addresses they gave the town hall. Three answers come back. The Mulders are in Rotterdam, poor and happy. The De Graafs are in America. The third letter is from a woman who rents rooms in the city: the widow Brink has died, alone. Nobody wants to come back. The last letter, from the Mulders, ends like this: *Life there is too good. We would rather be unhappy.*
Scrivete a tutte le famiglie partite, ag.short: Three replies come. The Mulders are poor and happy in Rotterdam, the De Graafs in America; the widow Brink has died alone in the city. Nobody will come back. *Life there is too good*, write the Mulders. *We would rather be unhappy.*

Il paese è in festa per il premio della.easy: The village is having a party for the province's prize. There are little flags, a band, and the mayor's speech on the stage in front of the Town Hall. Mayor Aldert Wessel is seventy but looks fifty. He talks for an hour and never looks at his notes. At the end everyone claps at the same moment, and stops at the same moment.
Il paese è in festa per il premio della.short: The village celebrates its prize. Mayor Wessel, seventy and looking fifty, speaks for an hour without notes. Everyone claps at the same moment, and stops at the same moment.

Dalla piazza si vede la torre della tenu.easy: From the square you can see the tower of the estate, with the iron chains that Lambert the master builder put around it some years ago. It has not moved at all. The children call it "the tower in prison".
Dalla piazza si vede la torre della tenu.short: From the square you see the estate's tower in its iron chains. The children call it "the tower in prison".

Nel punto della luce, nella torbiera, do.easy: In the bog, at the place where the light was and the stone sleeps, the water never freezes. In winter the skaters go around it and do not look.
Nel punto della luce, nella torbiera, do.short: Where the stone sleeps, the bog never freezes. The skaters go round it without looking.

Escono a mezzanotte, in sei, con le lant.easy: They go out at midnight, six of them, with lanterns and sticks, and knock at only one door. The Neighbour opens the door in a nightshirt. It is awake, as if it was waiting for them. It does not fight. They take it to the dyke, make it sit on the bank and wait with it until morning, in silence. At dawn, where it sat, there is a pile of wet peat.
Escono a mezzanotte, in sei, con le lant.short: Six of them knock at one door at midnight. The Neighbour opens, awake, as if expecting them, and sits with them on the dyke till dawn. At dawn there is only wet peat.

Escono a mezzanotte, con le lanterne ele.easy: They go out at midnight with electric lamps and a hunting gun, and knock at only one door. Hendrik Tammer, who fought in the war, goes in first. The Neighbour is sitting at the kitchen table, dressed, with its hands in its lap. It says only: "Be quiet, the children are sleeping." In the morning there is a pile of peat on the chair.
Escono a mezzanotte, con le lanterne ele.short: At midnight Hendrik Tammer, back from the war, goes in first. The Neighbour sits dressed at the kitchen table: "Quietly, the children are asleep." By morning, peat on the chair.

La scuola di {0} si fa nella sala dietro.easy: The {0} school is in the hall behind the church. The teacher, Neeltje Borg, is a young woman from the city with glasses and a soft voice. She stops you at the door with a folder under her arm. Every Monday, she says, she asks the children to draw their dream from Sunday night. She learned this exercise at teachers' college. Here in {1}, half the children give her an empty page. They say they do not dream. The other half always draw the same thing: the bog at night, with a light in the middle.
La scuola di {0} si fa nella sala dietro.short: Every Monday Miss Borg, the young teacher, has the children draw Sunday night's dream. Half hand in blank sheets: they do not dream. The other half always draw the bog at night, with a light in the middle.

Joost Maas sfoglia i disegni nel suo stu.easy: In his surgery, Joost Maas looks at the drawings one by one, in silence. Then he puts them in order, from the oldest to the newest, and shows you something you did not see before. In every drawing, week after week, the light in the middle of the bog gets a little bigger. Joost closes the folder and says it is a case of mass suggestion. His hands are shaking.
Joost Maas sfoglia i disegni nel suo stu.short: Dr Maas sorts the drawings by date and shows you: week by week, the light in the bog grows bigger. Mass suggestion, he says, closing the folder. His hands are shaking.

La maestra ti ringrazia, sollevata: avev.easy: The teacher thanks you. She is relieved: she was afraid that she was the strange one. She tells you a secret: since she came to {0}, she is the only person in the village who still dreams every night. Bad dreams, she says, but they are hers.
La maestra ti ringrazia, sollevata: avev.short: The teacher is relieved: she feared she was the strange one. She is the only one in {0} who still dreams every night. Bad dreams, but her own.

La maestra ti mostra il registro di clas.easy: The teacher shows you the class register. There is a small cross next to some names. The children with the empty pages are the best in the class. They are on time, tidy and polite. They do not fight, they do not cry, and they never hurt their knees. Next to some names there is a second, smaller cross. The teacher says that the parents signed the school reports with the same handwriting as the child.
La maestra ti mostra il registro di clas.short: The blank-sheet children are the best in class: punctual, polite, never in tears, never a grazed knee. Some have a second cross: their parents signed the reports in the child's own handwriting.

Al Town Hall, nella sala piccola, si son.easy: At the Town Hall, in the small room, about ten people have come together: peat-cutters, two shop assistants, Siebe the gravedigger, who is old now, and Miss Borg the teacher. They want to keep watch at night, like Pastor Kalf once did. They say they have seen things: people walking to the bog at night in their nightshirts, with bare feet, and coming back dry in the morning. The council has already said no. There is no crime in {0}, they say, and a watch would frighten families. So they need someone from the estate, because the council will not dare to say no to the estate.
Al Town Hall, nella sala piccola, si son.short: A dozen villagers want to revive Pastor Kalf's night watch: they have seen barefoot sleepwalkers going to the bog and coming back dry. The council said no. With someone from the estate, it would not dare.

Accetti. Ti consegnano la lanterna più g.easy: You say yes. They give you the biggest lantern, a whistle and the list of who watches when. On the first night nothing happens. On the second night, at one o'clock, on the road along the dyke, you meet a man in a nightshirt. He is walking towards the bog with his eyes open. You call his name. He stops, turns, says hello, and goes home.
Accetti. Ti consegnano la lanterna più g.short: You lead the Watch. On the second night, on the dyke, a man in a nightshirt walks open-eyed towards the bog. You call his name. He stops, greets you, and goes home.

Parli a lungo, con calma, e alla fine li.easy: You talk calmly for a long time, and in the end they agree: a watch would divide the village, and the village is all they have. They leave one by one, disappointed. Miss Borg is the last to go. At the door she asks if you also still dream at night.
Parli a lungo, con calma, e alla fine li.short: You persuade them a watch would divide the village. They leave disappointed. At the door, Miss Borg asks whether you still dream at night.

Al cimitero sull'argine, seduto su una t.easy: At the cemetery on the dyke, Gerrit Tammer, Fokke's son, is sitting on a grave. He is thirty-five, with wide shoulders and the face of a man who does not sleep. He cuts peat like his father, but alone, with the old spade, the one from before. He says he comes here every Sunday to visit his mother's grave. She died last year. She was the only person who understood him.
Al cimitero sull'argine, seduto su una t.short: Gerrit Tammer, Fokke's son, thirty-five and sleepless, sits on his mother's grave. He cuts peat alone, with the old spade. She was the only one who understood him.

\"Mio padre non è mio padre\", dice. \"L.easy: "My father is not my father," he says. "I have known it since I was ten. He brought me up, he loved me, and he never hit me. My real father hit me. He was a drunk and a violent man. But he was my father." He gives you the spade. Its handle is worn by the hands of two generations of Tammers. "Someone must dig. I cannot do it alone."
\"Mio padre non è mio padre\", dice. \"L.short: "My father is not my father. He loved me and never hit me. My real father was a violent drunk. But he was my father." He holds out the spade. "Someone has to dig. I cannot do it alone."

Prendi la vanga. Gerrit ti stringe la ma.easy: You take the spade. Gerrit shakes your hand for a long time. His hand is warm and rough. "We will dig together," he says. "At the place where the light was. When the peat is dry, at the end of the summer. The other peat-cutters do not go there. They say the peat under there is warm."
Prendi la vanga. Gerrit ti stringe la ma.short: Gerrit shakes your hand with his warm, rough one. "We will dig together, at the place of the light, when the peat is dry. The others will not go there: they say it is warm down there."

Gerrit ascolta, annuisce, e si rimette l.easy: Gerrit listens, nods and puts the spade back on his shoulder. He does not look offended. He looks tired. He walks away along the dyke, towards the bog, alone. The next Sunday he does not come to the cemetery. Or the Sunday after that.
Gerrit ascolta, annuisce, e si rimette l.short: Gerrit nods and shoulders his spade, more tired than offended, and walks alone towards the bog. He does not come back the next Sunday, nor the one after.

Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder is much older than the age to stop working, but he still climbs on roofs. The council has told him to knock down the empty houses of the families who left. But his builders do not want to go inside. They say it is not because the walls are unsafe. It is because someone is in there. In the beds, under the mouldy blankets, there is always a shape, like a sleeping person. When you lift the blanket, it is peat.
Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.short: The council has ordered Lambert to demolish the empty houses, but his men will not go in. In every bed, under the mouldy blankets, lies a shape like a sleeper. Underneath, it is peat.

La casa dei Mulder è fredda e buia. Nell.easy: The Mulders' house is cold and dark. In the bedroom, under the blanket, there is a long, thin shape with its head on the pillow. You lift the blanket. It is black, wet peat, shaped like a sleeping man, with its hands together on its chest. On the bedside table there is a pair of glasses. They belong to old Mulder, who, people say, still wears them in Rotterdam.
La casa dei Mulder è fredda e buia. Nell.short: In the Mulders' bedroom, under the blanket, lies a man of black peat, hands folded on his chest. On the bedside table: old Mulder's spectacles. The ones he still wears in Rotterdam, they say.

Paghi il doppio, e i muratori lavorano i.easy: You pay twice the price, and the builders work fast without going inside. With ropes and horses they pull the walls down, all together, in a cloud of black dust. Lambert watches with his hands behind his back and no expression on his face. All day long the ruins smell of the bog.
Paghi il doppio, e i muratori lavorano i.short: You pay double, and ropes and horses bring the walls down in a cloud of black dust. Lambert watches without expression. All day the rubble smells of the bog.

Al Laborer's Union, che ormai è un uffic.easy: The Laborer's Union is now a clean office with white walls and a picture of the queen. The council clerk hires workers there for the town's building work. He is Piet Brink, the widow's son. He is a young man of twenty-five, tidy and polite, with an amazing memory. He knows the name of every worker, every wife and every child. He has never missed a day of work because he was ill.
Al Laborer's Union, che ormai è un uffic.short: The council clerk at the Laborer's Union is Piet Brink, the widow's son: twenty-five, neat, polite, with a prodigious memory. He has never had a day off sick.

Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once. "One of your family was there," he says kindly, "that day at the bog, with my mother. She was calling me. I heard her, you know. But I was sleeping too well to answer."
Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.short: He recognises your family at once. "One of yours was at the bog with my mother that day. She called me. I heard her. But I was sleeping too well to answer."

Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once. "Midwife Maas examined me when I was a boy, because one of your family asked her to," he says kindly. "She wrote a sentence in her Register. I have always wondered what it said."
Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.short: He recognises your family at once. "Midwife Maas examined me as a boy, because one of yours asked. She wrote a sentence in her Register. I have always wondered what."

Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.easy: When he sees you, he knows your family at once, and he thanks you. "One of your family told my mother that I had grown up. They were right. She never believed it, poor woman. She died in the city, alone. I wrote to her every week."
Quando ti vede, riconosce subito la tua.short: He recognises your family and thanks you: "One of yours told my mother I had grown up. She never believed it. She died alone in the city. I wrote every week."

Piet parla della vedova Brink con affett.easy: Piet talks about the widow Brink with love, for a long time, and he never stops to think. He remembers everything: her recipes, her songs, her angry moments, the day she threw a wooden shoe at him. He remembers everything except one thing: he cannot say how he felt when she left. He really tries to remember, with a frown. Then he smiles: "Nothing bad, I think."
Piet parla della vedova Brink con affett.short: Piet remembers everything about his mother, even the clog she threw at him. Everything except what he felt when she left. He frowns, honestly trying. Then he smiles: "Nothing bad, I think."

Piet li assume tutti, subito, con la pag.easy: Piet gives them all a job, immediately, with full pay. He asks for nothing in return. The next day the workers of the Watch are working on the dyke with the others. In the evening they go home tired, and at night they sleep.
Piet li assume tutti, subito, con la pag.short: Piet hires them all at full pay, asking nothing back. Now the Watch works on the dyke all day, and at night they sleep.

Alla Traveling Caravan, tra i carri dei.easy: At the Traveling Caravan, among the sellers' carts, there is a covered cart with a whole family sitting on it in silence. It is the Mulders. They have come back from Rotterdam for a week to take their things from their empty house. Old Mulder's hands are damaged from work at the port, and his glasses are broken and held together with wire. When he sees you, he gets down from the cart and takes you away from the others.
Alla Traveling Caravan, tra i carri dei.short: The Mulders are back from Rotterdam for a week, to fetch their things. Old Mulder, his hands ruined by the docks, his spectacles mended with wire, takes you aside.

\"Non bevete l'acqua\", dice. \"E se ved.easy: "Do not drink the water," he says. "And if you see someone with your face, do not look into their eyes. We left when my wife said goodnight to me in her normal voice, but with cold hands. That evening I took the children and went away. She did not come with us. She writes to us. She says she is fine."
\"Non bevete l'acqua\", dice. \"E se ved.short: "Do not drink the water. If you see someone with your face, do not look them in the eye. My wife said goodnight with cold hands, and I took the children and left. She writes. She says she is well."

I Mulder dormono alla tenuta per una set.easy: The Mulders sleep at the estate for a week. They drink only beer. In the evenings old Mulder sits with you by the fire and tells you what {0} was like before the two lights: dirty, poor, noisy, full of people who argued and sang. When he leaves, he gives you a list of names: the people he thinks are still "real".
I Mulder dormono alla tenuta per una set.short: The Mulders stay a week, drinking only beer. By the fire old Mulder remembers {0} before the lights: dirty, poor, full of fights and songs. He leaves you a list of those still "real".

La signora Mulder, ti dice il vecchio, v.easy: The old man tells you that Mrs Mulder still lives in the empty house. She has never left it. He has not gone inside these days: he sends the children to get their things. But tonight he will go in, to say goodbye to her. The next day the Mulders' cart leaves at dawn. On the seat next to the old man there is a woman in a shawl, with her hands in her lap, smiling at everyone.
La signora Mulder, ti dice il vecchio, v.short: Mrs Mulder, the old man says, never left the empty house. Tonight he will go in to say goodbye. At dawn the cart leaves, and beside him sits a woman in a shawl, smiling at everyone.

Ho misurato la temperatura di centosessa.easy: In six years I have measured the temperature of one hundred and sixty people in {0}, with a very exact thermometer from Leiden. One hundred and twenty of them have an average temperature of thirty-four point eight degrees. My books say that at thirty-four point eight a person shivers, goes mad and dies. These hundred and twenty are very healthy. They do not shiver. They do not get ill. They never come to see me, except when they bring someone who has a fever.
Ho misurato la temperatura di centosessa.short: In six years I have measured one hundred and sixty villagers. One hundred and twenty average thirty-four point eight degrees, a temperature that kills. They are perfectly well, and never ill.

Ho cominciato a pensare che mia madre av.easy: I am starting to think that my mother was right. I do not write it all out. I just write it.
Ho cominciato a pensare che mia madre av.short: I begin to think my mother was right. I write only that.

Nel cassetto del Registro, sotto l'orolo.easy: In the drawer of the Register, under the broken watch that she kept there, I found her loose notes. There are names, dates and temperatures, and next to some names there is a small cross. I checked the crosses one by one. They were all right.
Nel cassetto del Registro, sotto l'orolo.short: Under her broken watch in the drawer I found her notes, with crosses beside some names. I checked every one. All correct.

La Ronda di {0} gira di notte, con le la.easy: {0}'s Watch walks around at night with lanterns. The council complains, very politely. In the village, during the day, people say hello to {1} as kindly as always. At night, when the Watch walks past, the windows stay dark.
La Ronda di {0} gira di notte, con le la.short: {0}'s Watch walks the night with lanterns. By day the village greets {1} as politely as ever. By night the windows stay dark as the Watch goes by.

{0} scava con Gerrit Tammer, nel punto d.easy: At the end of every summer, {0} digs with Gerrit Tammer at the place where the light was. People say the peat down there is warm, and sometimes, if you put your ear close, you can hear someone breathing. That is what people say.
{0} scava con Gerrit Tammer, nel punto d.short: Every late summer {0} digs with Gerrit Tammer at the place of the light. The peat there is warm, they say, and sometimes it breathes.

Dalla città mi scrive un collega del mus.easy: A colleague from the natural history museum writes to me from the city. Professor Ostrander has died. He was over ninety, he was not ill, and he was smiling. In his study they found a little velvet box inside a glass of water, and some peat on the armchair.
Dalla città mi scrive un collega del mus.short: Professor Ostrander has died past ninety, without illness, smiling. In his study: a velvet box in a glass of water, and peat on the armchair.

I nipoti del cane di Fokke Tammer, quell.easy: The grandchildren of Fokke Tammer's dog, the dog the estate took many years ago, still bark at the same people. I take them with me when I visit my patients. They are never wrong.
I nipoti del cane di Fokke Tammer, quell.short: The grandchildren of Fokke's old dog still bark at the same people. I take them on my rounds. They are never wrong.

Di notte la torbiera fuma, anche d'estat.easy: At night the bog smokes, even in summer. It is a low, white smoke. It rises from the place where the light was and spreads over the water, with no wind. People say that if you watch it too long, you do not want to go to bed any more. You go and sit on the dyke, and wait.
Di notte la torbiera fuma, anche d'estat.short: At night a low white smoke rises from the place of the light, even in summer. Watch it too long, they say, and you no longer want to sleep: you sit on the dyke, and wait.

Alla tenuta arrivano inviti a ogni festa.easy: The estate gets invitations to every party, every christening and every wedding. Everyone wants you. Everyone is waiting for you.
Alla tenuta arrivano inviti a ogni festa.short: Invitations to everything reach the estate. Everyone wants you. Everyone is waiting for you.

Alla tenuta non arriva più nessuno. La p.easy: Nobody comes to the estate now. They leave the letters at the gate. The milkman rings the bell and goes away before you open the door.
Alla tenuta non arriva più nessuno. La p.short: Nobody comes to the estate now. The post is left at the gate; the milkman rings and is gone.

Trijntje Kalf, la figlia del vecchio pas.easy: Trijntje Kalf, the old pastor's daughter, has played the church organ for twenty years. She is a small woman with long fingers and a perfect ear. She stops you after the service, under the porch. She says the choir sings too well. There are thirty voices, and none of them sings out of tune any more. Nobody coughs, nobody breathes at the wrong moment. They sing like one single person. Every Sunday, at the end of the hymn, the silence lasts exactly four bars. Then they all sit down at the same time. She never taught them to do that.
Trijntje Kalf, la figlia del vecchio pas.short: Trijntje Kalf, the organist, says the choir sings too well: thirty voices like one, never a cough, never a wrong breath. After every hymn, exactly four bars of silence, then they all sit at once. She never taught them that.

Canti con loro, e non hai mai cantato co.easy: You sing with them, and you have never sung so well. Your voice rests on the others like a boat on the water, and for the whole hymn you do not have to think about anything. It is beautiful. When the hymn ends, you sit down with all the others, exactly after four bars. You only notice it later.
Canti con loro, e non hai mai cantato co.short: You sing with them, better than ever, thinking of nothing. When the hymn ends you sit down with everyone, exactly four bars later. You notice only afterwards.

Ti siedi in fondo, con gli occhi chiusi,.easy: You sit at the back with your eyes closed and listen. Between the verses, half of the choir does not breathe. They do not need to. At the organ, Trijntje turns towards you. For a moment she plays a wrong note, on purpose, loudly. Nobody in the choir follows her mistake.
Ti siedi in fondo, con gli occhi chiusi,.short: Eyes closed at the back, you hear it: half the choir never takes a breath. Trijntje plays one loud wrong note on purpose. Nobody follows her.

Al Park, di notte, vicino allo stagno, t.easy: At night, in the Park, near the pond, six people are waiting for you. You know them all: Lambert the master builder, Piet Brink, Jaap Mol the smith, two shop assistants and the miller. They are kind. They ask you for {0}'s stone. Not for them, they say, but for the village. The stone suffers when it is far from water. And when it suffers, they feel it. They ask you to think about it. They have time.
Al Park, di notte, vicino allo stagno, t.short: Six villagers wait for you by the pond at night, all kind. They want {0}'s stone, for the village: it suffers far from water, and they feel it. Think about it. They have time.

Al Park, di notte, l'acqua dello stagno.easy: At night, in the Park, the water of the pond shines with a low, green light. It comes from the bottom, from the canal that goes to the bog. Down there, where the light was, the stone sank. The peat-cutters say that with tall boots and a rope you could pull it out.
Al Park, di notte, l'acqua dello stagno.short: At night the pond glows green from the canal that leads to the bog, where the stone sank. With tall boots and a rope, say the peat-cutters, it could be fished out.

La notte dopo la porti all'argine, nel s.easy: The next night you take it to the dyke in its sack. A hundred people are waiting for you, with lanterns, in silence. They take it carefully and pass it from hand to hand down to the bank. Then they carry it back into the bog in a procession, singing the Sunday hymn with one voice. When the stone sinks, they all stop singing at the same moment and go home.
La notte dopo la porti all'argine, nel s.short: A hundred silent people take the stone from you at the dyke and carry it into the bog, singing the Sunday hymn in one voice. When it sinks, they all stop at once and go home.

La nascondi in cantina, dietro le botti,.easy: You hide it in the cellar, behind the barrels, in an iron box with two padlocks. For a week, every night, someone knocks at the door of the estate. Three soft knocks. When you open the door, nobody is there. But on the step there is always a pool of dark water, and in the morning it is gone.
La nascondi in cantina, dietro le botti,.short: You lock it in the cellar. For a week, every night, three soft knocks at the door. Nobody there, only a pool of dark water on the step, gone by morning.

Entri nella torbiera fino al petto, con.easy: You walk into the bog up to your chest, with a rope around your waist and a lantern. The water is ice cold, and for a moment you think there is no bottom. Then you find it in the soft peat: warm, smooth, alive under your fingers. When you pull it out, the whole bog sighs softly, like a person turning over in their sleep.
Entri nella torbiera fino al petto, con.short: Chest-deep in icy water, you find the stone in the soft peat, warm and alive. As you pull it out, the whole bog sighs like a sleeper turning over.

Torni a casa con le scarpe bagnate e un.easy: You go home with wet shoes and a thought that will not go away: down there, at the bottom, something knew you were there, and it let you go.
Torni a casa con le scarpe bagnate e un.short: You go home with wet shoes, sure that something down there knew you were there, and let you go.

Al cimitero, il becchino Siebe, vecchiss.easy: At the cemetery, Siebe the gravedigger, who is very old now, calls you over with his hand. For some nights, he says, when the bog smokes, he has heard breathing under the ground. Not in the graves, but between the graves, where nobody is buried. It is a very slow, deep breath, one each minute, like someone in a heavy sleep. He takes you to the place, near the new wall. You put your ear on the grass. Silence. Then, after a minute, something breathes under the ground.
Al cimitero, il becchino Siebe, vecchiss.short: Old Siebe hears breathing underground between the graves, one slow breath a minute. You put your ear to the grass. Silence. Then, under the earth, something breathes.

Scavate fino a un metro, con la lanterna.easy: You dig down one metre, with the lantern. You find dark, warm water and nothing else. Siebe says it is the peat water, which goes up and down with the moon and makes that sound. He says it without looking at you. Then he fills the hole quickly and puts a cross with no name on top.
Scavate fino a un metro, con la lanterna.short: A yard down you find only dark, lukewarm water. The peat water rising with the moon, says Siebe, not looking at you. He fills the hole fast and plants a nameless cross on it.

La Ronda veglia tutta la notte nel cimit.easy: The Watch stays in the cemetery all night, six people around a fire, with blankets. That night the breathing is silent. But at dawn, when they stand up to leave, the grass around the fire is wet in a perfect circle, as if someone under the ground had come closer to get warm.
La Ronda veglia tutta la notte nel cimit.short: The Watch keeps vigil all night by a fire. The breathing stays silent. But at dawn the grass round the fire is wet in a perfect circle, as if someone below had come closer to get warm.

Al Farmer's Market, il banco della torba.easy: At the Farmer's Market the black peat stall is still there, and Fokke Tammer is still behind it. He is over seventy, with white hair, and he still cuts the peat himself every morning at dawn. He does not wear bandages now. His hands are smooth, with no hard skin and no lines. He knows you at once, and asks about all your family, alive and dead, one by one, by name. He does not get one wrong.
Al Farmer's Market, il banco della torba.short: Fokke Tammer, past seventy, still sells his black peat. His hands are smooth, without lines. He asks after all your family, living and dead, by name, and gets none wrong.

Fokke sospira. Gerrit è un bravo ragazzo.easy: Fokke sighs. Gerrit is a good boy, he says, but he is like his mother: he worries too much. Fokke loves him anyway, as a father must. Then he kindly asks you to tell Gerrit to stop digging. "The peat belongs to everyone," he says. "But the bottom belongs to the ones who sleep there."
Fokke sospira. Gerrit è un bravo ragazzo.short: Gerrit worries too much, like his mother, Fokke sighs, but he loves him. Tell him to stop digging. "The peat belongs to everyone. But the bottom belongs to those who sleep there."

Fokke ci pensa. Ricorda la luce, dice: b.easy: Fokke thinks. He says he remembers the light: white, with no heat. And the stone in the water, hot like a stove, and the pain in his hands. Then he remembers bending down to look at the bottom, because under the stone someone was sleeping, someone with his face. "He looked so tired," Fokke says. "I told him: sleep, I will do it." Then he gives you your change, exact to the penny.
Fokke ci pensa. Ricorda la luce, dice: b.short: Fokke remembers the light, the hot stone, the pain. And under the stone, someone asleep with his face. "He looked so tired. I told him: sleep, I will do it." He gives you your change, exact.

Al Blacksmith, Jaap Mol batte il ferro c.easy: At the Blacksmith, Jaap Mol hits the iron as hard as he did thirty years ago. His apprentice, a Van Dam boy of sixteen with red ears, stops you at the door. He wants to leave, he says, but he does not know where to go. His master never makes mistakes, never gets angry and never gets tired. He corrects the boy with endless patience. Yesterday he told the boy that soon he too will stop making mistakes: he only needs to go into the canal one night, like Jaap did. The boy is afraid of water.
Al Blacksmith, Jaap Mol batte il ferro c.short: Jaap Mol's apprentice, a red-eared Van Dam boy, wants to leave. His master never errs, never tires, and has told him one night's bathe in the canal will cure his mistakes too. The boy is afraid of water.

Il ragazzo dei Van Dam si chiama Kees. L.easy: The Van Dam boy's name is Kees. He works in the tower, cleans the ring and polishes the brass. He makes every mistake that can be made: he spills the oil, burns himself and breaks a piece of glass. It is wonderful to have him around. Jaap Mol does not come to take him back. The next week he only sends a present: a new hammer, perfect.
Il ragazzo dei Van Dam si chiama Kees. L.short: The boy is Kees. In the tower he spills oil, burns himself, breaks a pane: a joy to have around. Jaap Mol sends only a present: a perfect new hammer.

Il ragazzo abbassa gli occhi e torna all.easy: The boy looks down and goes back to the anvil. A week later you see him at the market. He stands straight and calm, his hands are clean and his ears are pale. He says hello to you by name. He thanks you for your advice.
Il ragazzo abbassa gli occhi e torna all.short: The boy goes back to the anvil. A week later, at the market, he is calm, clean-handed, his ears pale. He greets you by name and thanks you for your advice.

Il consiglio, all'unanimità, ha il piace.easy: The whole council has voted, and is happy to make the family of the estate honorary citizens of {0}. The family will get money every year and a seat in the front row at all ceremonies. This is to thank them for forty years of service to science and to the village.
Il consiglio, all'unanimità, ha il piace.short: The council unanimously makes the family of the estate honorary citizens of {0}, with a yearly pension and front-row seats, for forty years of service.

Il consiglio confida che la famiglia vor.easy: In return, the council hopes that the family will stop doing anything that could disturb the peace of the people: night watches, digging in the bog, measurements that nobody asked for. In {0}, peace belongs to everyone.
Il consiglio confida che la famiglia vor.short: In return, the council trusts the family will give up night watches, digging and unrequested measurements. In {0}, peace is a common good.

La cerimonia si tiene al Town Hall, con.easy: The ceremony is at the Town Hall, with the band and flowers. The mayor pins a silver medal with the village crest on the chest of each heir, and shakes hands with each of them, with his cold hand. The money arrives on time on the first day of every month. The lanterns of the Watch stay hanging in the cellar.
La cerimonia si tiene al Town Hall, con.short: At the Town Hall the mayor pins a silver medal on each heir and shakes their hands with his cold one. The pension comes every month. The Watch's lanterns stay in the cellar.

Rispondete con una lettera cortese e bre.easy: You answer with a short, polite letter. The mayor is not offended. He thanks you for being honest, tells you the offer is open "for ever", and the next week he sends you a basket of fruit anyway. From that day, at the market, the sellers always serve you last, with a smile.
Rispondete con una lettera cortese e bre.short: You decline politely. The mayor thanks you, keeps the offer open "for ever", and sends fruit. From then on the market serves you last, always smiling.

Gerrit Tammer scava ogni notte, nel punt.easy: Every night Gerrit Tammer digs at the place where the light was, with a lantern and his father's spade. The council has sent him two very polite warning letters. In the tidy village of {0}, at the edge of the bog, a wound of black peat gets bigger every week.
Gerrit Tammer scava ogni notte, nel punt.short: Every night Gerrit Tammer digs at the place of the light. Two polite warnings from the council. At the edge of tidy {0}, a wound of black peat widens every week.

Al Park, dove lo stagno si apre nel cana.easy: At the Park, where the pond meets the canal of the bog, Gerrit Tammer has built a wall of sandbags and taken the water out of an area as big as a room. He works with three peat-cutters from the Watch. They have no shirts on, and they stand in mud up to their knees. They have cut the peat into bricks, layer after layer, two metres deep. Gerrit says the peat down there is warm. And soft, like a blanket.
Al Park, dove lo stagno si apre nel cana.short: Behind a dam of sandbags, Gerrit Tammer and three men of the Watch have dug two metres into the peat. Down there, Gerrit says, it is warm, and soft as a blanket.

{0} è con loro, con la vecchia vanga dei.easy: {0} is with them, with the old Tammer spade. Every stroke is easier than the one before.
{0} è con loro, con la vecchia vanga dei.short: {0} digs with them. Each stroke is easier than the last.

Scendi nella buca. La torba, sotto la va.easy: You go down into the hole. The peat is as soft as fresh bread under the spade. Then the blade touches something soft and smooth that is not peat. Gerrit grabs your wrist. His face is white. "Tomorrow," he says. "When it is light. And with everyone."
Scendi nella buca. La torba, sotto la va.short: The peat gives like fresh bread. Then the spade touches something smooth that is not peat. Gerrit grips your wrist, white-faced: "Tomorrow. In daylight. With everyone."

Porti pane, aringhe, birra, e resti sull.easy: You bring bread, herring and beer, and you stay on the dyke with a lantern to keep watch. Around midnight you see a line of people coming from the village road, in silence, with their hands in their pockets. They stop fifty steps from the hole and watch. At dawn they all leave together.
Porti pane, aringhe, birra, e resti sull.short: Keeping watch on the dyke, at midnight you see a silent line of figures, hands in pockets, stop fifty paces from the pit and watch. At dawn they all leave together.

Al Farmer's Market, Fokke Tammer vende l.easy: At the Farmer's Market, Fokke Tammer sells his black peat, as he does every day, calm and polite. On the other side of the square his son Gerrit leans against the wall and watches him. His hands are dirty with peat and his shirt is torn. They have not spoken for a year. Sometimes Fokke smiles at him. Gerrit does not smile back.
Al Farmer's Market, Fokke Tammer vende l.short: Fokke sells his black peat, serene. Across the square his son Gerrit, peat-stained and torn, watches him. They have not spoken for a year. Fokke smiles. Gerrit does not.

Fokke ti chiede, con dolcezza, di parlar.easy: Fokke gently asks you to talk to his son. He is afraid Gerrit will get hurt down there in the hole. He is afraid for him, he says, like every father. And he is afraid of what Gerrit will find: "Some things keep better if nobody takes them out." He gives you a brick of black peat for your stove.
Fokke ti chiede, con dolcezza, di parlar.short: Fokke asks you to talk to his son: he fears for him, like any father, and fears what he will find. "Some things keep better if nobody pulls them out." He gives you a brick of black peat.

Gerrit non guarda te: guarda il padre. \.easy: Gerrit does not look at you. He looks at his father. "My father snored," he says. "He snored so loudly that the neighbours could hear him. This one sleeps like a stone and makes no sound. For forty years." Then he moves away from the wall and walks towards the bog with his spade on his shoulder.
Gerrit non guarda te: guarda il padre. \.short: Gerrit watches his father. "My father snored so loud the neighbours heard. This one has slept without a sound for forty years." He shoulders his spade and heads for the bog.

Al Town Hall, il dottor Joost Maas ha or.easy: At the Town Hall, Dr Joost Maas has organised vaccinations: smallpox has arrived in the villages nearby. Half of the village is waiting in line in front of his table, calm and patient, with their sleeves already rolled up. Joost vaccinates everyone, and secretly he takes everyone's temperature too. When it is your turn, he shows you the thermometer and quietly asks if he may.
Al Town Hall, il dottor Joost Maas ha or.short: Dr Maas is vaccinating half the village against smallpox, and secretly taking every temperature. At your turn he shows you the thermometer and softly asks permission.

Ti ringrazia, sottovoce, per i disegni d.easy: He quietly thanks you for the teacher's drawings. Since that day, he says, he cannot stop counting.
Ti ringrazia, sottovoce, per i disegni d.short: He thanks you quietly for the drawings: since then he cannot stop counting.

Trentasei e otto. Joost guarda il termom.easy: Thirty-six point eight. Joost looks at the thermometer, then at you, and gives a sigh of relief so loud that the people in the line turn around. He shakes your hand: it is warm. Then he goes back to his vaccinations, and he hums all afternoon.
Trentasei e otto. Joost guarda il termom.short: Thirty-six point eight. Joost sighs so loudly with relief that the queue turns round. He shakes your warm hand, and hums all afternoon.

Joost non insiste. Annota il rifiuto sul.easy: Joost does not insist. He writes in the Register that you said no, with the date and the time, and a question mark next to it. The people in the line behind you smile at you as if they understand.
Joost non insiste. Annota il rifiuto sul.short: Joost writes your refusal in the Register, with a question mark. The queue behind you smiles, understanding.

Joost ride, nervoso. Poi, davanti a te,.easy: Joost laughs nervously. Then, in front of you, he puts the thermometer under his tongue. He waits. He looks at it. He shakes it and puts it back. He looks at it again. Thirty-six point six. He sits down with his hands on his knees and stays like that for a while, like a man who has just won a bet that he did not want to make.
Joost ride, nervoso. Poi, davanti a te,.short: Joost laughs nervously and takes his own, twice. Thirty-six point six. He sits down, hands on his knees, like a man who has won a bet he never wanted to make.

Il pastore Ewout Kalf ha novant'anni e s.easy: Pastor Ewout Kalf is ninety and he is dying, in his house behind the church, with his daughter Trijntje next to the bed. He has asked for you. His hands are warm, and his voice is as thin as paper. Before he dies he wants to know only one thing: how many there are. He does not say who. He does not need to.
Il pastore Ewout Kalf ha novant'anni e s.short: Pastor Kalf, ninety and dying, has sent for you. His hands are warm, his voice thin as paper. He wants to know only one thing: how many there are. He need not say who.

Ti riconosce, o riconosce in te il genit.easy: He knows you, or he sees in you the parent who agreed with him on the church steps, many years ago. He smiles.
Ti riconosce, o riconosce in te il genit.short: He sees in you the parent who agreed with him on the church steps. He smiles.

Ti riconosce, o riconosce in te il genit.easy: He knows you, or he sees in you the parent who argued with him on the church steps, many years ago. He reaches out his hand to you anyway.
Ti riconosce, o riconosce in te il genit.short: He sees in you the parent who argued with him on the church steps. He holds out his hand anyway.

Gli dici il numero di Joost Maas: più de.easy: You tell him Joost Maas's number: more than half. The pastor closes his eyes. Then he tells Trijntje to keep playing the organ, always, every Sunday, and to play one wrong note, only one, every time. "Then they will know you are still there." He dies at dawn. At the funeral the choir sings perfectly.
Gli dici il numero di Joost Maas: più de.short: More than half, you tell him. He closes his eyes, and asks Trijntje to play one wrong note every Sunday: "So they will know you are still there." He dies at dawn. At the funeral the choir sings perfectly.

Gli dici che sono pochi, e che diminuisc.easy: You tell him there are only a few, and fewer every year. The pastor looks at you for a long time, with tears in his eyes, and thanks you for the lie. "It was kind," he says. "That is how you know them now: they are kind." He dies at dawn. At the funeral Trijntje does not say hello to you.
Gli dici che sono pochi, e che diminuisc.short: Few, you tell him. He thanks you for the lie, tearful: "It was kind. That is how you know them now: by their kindness." He dies at dawn. Trijntje ignores you at the funeral.

Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.easy: At the Builder's Office, Lambert the master builder has put a map of the village on the wall, with red crosses on it. They show the houses that are sinking: three in one year, all near the bog, all in the same direction, towards Gerrit Tammer's dig. The walls crack, the floors lean, and in the end the house falls in, slowly, as if the ground under it were empty. Lambert says it is because of the dig. He asks the family of the estate, "who have so much influence", to close it.
Al Builder's Office il capomastro Lamber.short: Lambert's map shows three sinking houses, all in a line towards Gerrit Tammer's dig, as if hollowed out from below. He asks the family of the estate, "who have such influence", to have the dig closed.

Gerrit obbedisce, a denti stretti. Per u.easy: Gerrit obeys, but he is angry. For a month the hole fills with water, and the soft peat closes again over what was under it. Lambert thanks you and gives you the map with the crosses. That month the houses stop sinking.
Gerrit obbedisce, a denti stretti. Per u.short: Gerrit obeys, furious. The pit fills with water and the peat closes over what lay below. That month, the houses stop sinking.

Nelle cantine delle case crollate, tra l.easy: In the cellars of the fallen houses, among the broken bricks, the floor has broken open. Under it there is a hole in the peat, long and narrow, like a bed. Nobody is inside. But at the bottom the shape of a body is still warm. And from there a track as wide as a man goes towards the bog, as if someone, or something, was dragged along it.
Nelle cantine delle case crollate, tra l.short: Under each collapsed cellar lies a hollow in the peat shaped like a bed. Empty, but the print of a body is still warm, and a trail as wide as a man leads off towards the bog.

Chiamato all'alba allo scavo di Gerrit T.easy: They called me at dawn to Gerrit Tammer's dig, at the Park. There were Gerrit, the peat-cutters of the Watch, some members of the family of the estate, and me.
Chiamato all'alba allo scavo di Gerrit T.short: Called at dawn to Gerrit Tammer's dig. Present: Gerrit, the Watch, some of the estate family, and myself.

Sotto due metri di torba, in una cavità.easy: Under two metres of peat, in a hollow as soft as a bed, there is a man. He has white skin and black hair, and he wears the clothes of a peat-cutter from fifty years ago. His hands are together on his chest. There are new burns on his palms, not yet healed. His body temperature is thirty-one degrees. His heart beats four times a minute. He breathes once a minute, deeply and regularly. The man is asleep.
Sotto due metri di torba, in una cavità.short: Two metres down, in a hollow soft as a bed, lies a man in the clothes of fifty years ago, fresh burns on his palms. Thirty-one degrees, four heartbeats a minute, one breath. He is asleep.

L'uomo è Fokke Tammer, all'età di quaran.easy: The man is Fokke Tammer, at about forty years old. His son Gerrit knows him. Gerrit has fallen on his knees in the mud and cannot stand up. I know him too, from the burns: my mother put bandages on them. The other Fokke Tammer, who is eighty-eight, is at the Farmer's Market right now, behind his stall, serving his customers.
L'uomo è Fokke Tammer, all'età di quaran.short: It is Fokke Tammer, aged about forty. Gerrit kneels in the mud and cannot rise. I know the burns: my mother dressed them. The eighty-eight-year-old Fokke is at his market stall right now.

**Gli originali non sono morti. Dormono.easy: **The real people are not dead. They are sleeping in the peat, kept just as they were on the day they were taken. The ones who walk around {0} are something else.**
**Gli originali non sono morti. Dormono.short: **The originals are not dead: they sleep in the peat. Those who walk {0} are something else.**

Gerrit vuole svegliarlo. Joost Maas dice.easy: Gerrit wants to wake him. Joost Maas says he does not know what would happen. A man who has slept in the peat for almost fifty years might die when he wakes up, or he might live in a worse way. And what would the other Fokke, the one at the market, do? Meanwhile, on the dyke, the people of the village are starting to arrive. They do not come closer. They wait.
Gerrit vuole svegliarlo. Joost Maas dice.short: Gerrit wants to wake him. Joost does not know what would happen, to this Fokke or to the other. On the dyke the villagers have begun to gather. They come no closer. They wait.

Lo tirano fuori in sei, avvolto nelle co.easy: Six people lift him out, wrapped in blankets, and carry him to Joost Maas's surgery, next to the stove. It takes three days. On the third day Fokke Tammer opens his eyes. He looks at the ceiling, then at Gerrit, who is almost sixty and has a grey beard, and asks who he is. Then he asks what year it is. Then he asks for gin.
Lo tirano fuori in sei, avvolto nelle co.short: They carry him to Joost's stove. On the third day Fokke opens his eyes, looks at grey-bearded Gerrit and asks who he is. Then what year it is. Then for gin.

Al Farmer's Market, quella mattina, l'al.easy: That morning, at the Farmer's Market, the other Fokke stops serving in the middle of a sentence. He leaves his stall and walks straight to the bog. Nobody follows him. In the evening he comes back, and the next day he opens his stall again as if nothing has happened. But he does not say hello to anyone by name any more.
Al Farmer's Market, quella mattina, l'al.short: That morning the other Fokke stops mid-sentence and walks straight to the bog. He is back by evening, and opens his stall next day as usual. But he no longer greets anyone by name.

Gerrit ricopre il padre con le sue mani,.easy: Crying, Gerrit covers his father with his own hands, brick by brick, like someone tucking in a blanket. Then he opens the wall of sandbags and lets the water come back. On the dyke the village people wait until the water covers everything. Then they all go home together, in silence. The next day, at the Farmer's Market, Fokke gives Gerrit a brick of black peat. Gerrit takes it.
Gerrit ricopre il padre con le sue mani,.short: Weeping, Gerrit covers his father brick by brick and lets the water back in. The villagers wait until it is all covered, then leave together. Next day Fokke gives Gerrit a brick of black peat. Gerrit takes it.

Scrivo l'ultima pagina della mia parte d.easy: I am writing the last page of my part of the Register. The war started last year. Our country is not fighting, but half of Europe is on fire, and the young people of {0} are leaving as volunteers: for the ambulances, for the factories, for the front. The children of the estate are leaving. My daughter Wilhelmina is leaving too. She has just become a doctor, and she says the front needs doctors more than we do here. She is right. I gave her my mother's watch, the broken one. It will bring her luck, or at least it will tell her the time when it stopped.
Scrivo l'ultima pagina della mia parte d.short: My last page. The war has come; our country is not in it, but {0}'s young volunteer for the front, the children of the estate among them. My daughter Wilhelmina, a doctor now, goes too. I gave her my mother's broken watch, for luck.

I partenti hanno bevuto tutti l'acqua de.easy: On the morning they left, everyone who was leaving drank the water from the fountain. It is the village's new custom: "so you will come back". But not Wil. Wil drank beer.
I partenti hanno bevuto tutti l'acqua de.short: Everyone leaving drank the fountain water, "so as to come back". Not Wil. Wil drank beer.

Fokke Tammer, quello vero, vive con suo.easy: The real Fokke Tammer lives with his son Gerrit in a house on the dyke. He drinks, swears and snores, and he does not know anyone in the village. He says they are all too kind. The other Fokke still sells his peat at the market, on the other side of the square. They never look at each other.
Fokke Tammer, quello vero, vive con suo.short: The real Fokke lives with Gerrit on the dyke, drinking, swearing, snoring. Everyone is too kind, he says. Across the square the other Fokke sells his peat. They never look at each other.

Sotto la torba, nel punto dello scavo, F.easy: Under the peat, at the place of the dig, Fokke Tammer is still sleeping. On Sundays Gerrit takes flowers there, instead of to his mother's grave.
Sotto la torba, nel punto dello scavo, F.short: Fokke Tammer still sleeps under the dig. On Sundays Gerrit brings flowers there, not to his mother's grave.

Al Town Hall si festeggiano i quarant'an.easy: At the Town Hall there is a party for Aldert Wessel's forty years as mayor of {0}. There are flowers, a new oil painting of him, and a choir of children in a line. The mayor is eighty and walks as straight as a soldier. The committee asks someone from the estate, "the oldest family in the village", to say a few kind words from the stage. The speech is already written on a sheet of paper. The clerk, Piet Brink, wrote it.
Al Town Hall si festeggiano i quarant'an.short: {0} celebrates forty years of Mayor Wessel, eighty and straight as a soldier. Someone from the estate, "the oldest family", is asked to speak. The clerk, Piet Brink, has already written the speech.

Sul tavolo d'onore, accanto alla torta,.easy: At the table of honour, next to the cake, there is an empty place with a card: *Mrs Wessel*. The mayor explains that his wife is still at her sister's in the city, and she has written to say sorry. The letter is on the plate. It is in the mayor's handwriting.
Sul tavolo d'onore, accanto alla torta,.short: Beside the cake an empty place is laid for *Mrs Wessel*, still at her sister's. Her letter of apology lies on the plate, in the mayor's handwriting.

Leggi il discorso: è perfetto, caldo, se.easy: You read the speech. It is perfect and warm, and every word is right. While you read, you notice that the people in the hall are moving their lips with you. They know it by heart. At the end they all clap at the same moment, and the mayor hugs you, cold and full of emotion.
Leggi il discorso: è perfetto, caldo, se.short: You read the perfect speech, and the whole hall mouths it with you: they know it by heart. They clap as one, and the mayor embraces you, cold and moved.

Metti da parte il foglio e parli della s.easy: You put the paper away and talk about Mrs Wessel: her laugh like a hen's, her terrible hats, and her fights with her husband, which people could hear from the square. You tell them what {0} was like when people argued. The hall listens to you in perfect silence. The mayor smiles the whole time. When you finish, an old woman at the back of the hall is crying. She is the only one.
Metti da parte il foglio e parli della s.short: You speak instead of Mrs Wessel: her cackle, her awful hats, the rows heard across the square. The hall listens in perfect silence; the mayor smiles throughout. At the back, one old woman cries. Only one.

Declini con garbo: la famiglia della ten.easy: You say no politely: the family of the estate is not good at speeches. The committee does not insist. Instead, the clerk Piet Brink speaks, with no paper and no pauses, for exactly twenty minutes. At the end the mayor hugs him like a son.
Declini con garbo: la famiglia della ten.short: You decline. Piet Brink speaks instead, without notes, for exactly twenty minutes. The mayor embraces him like a son.

Al cimitero, nella casetta degli attrezz.easy: At the cemetery, in the tool shed next to the gate, Siebe the gravedigger is dying. He is ninety-one. He lies on a small bed, with his short leg wrapped in a blanket. He has asked for someone from the estate. From under the mattress he takes out an old school notebook, dirty and creased, and puts it in your hand. For fifty years, he says, every time he dug a grave and found water, he looked down. And every time he saw a face down there in the peat, he wrote it down. Name, date, depth.
Al cimitero, nella casetta degli attrezz.short: Siebe, ninety-one and dying in the tool shed, gives you a greasy exercise book. For fifty years, whenever he saw a face in the water of a fresh grave, he wrote it down: name, date, depth.

La prima pagina è del 1868: *la moglie d.easy: The first page is from 1868: *the miller's wife, third grave, under the coffin*. Your family was there.
La prima pagina è del 1868: *la moglie d.short: The first page, 1868: *the miller's wife, third grave, under the coffin*. Your family was there.

Le pagine sono quaranta. I nomi sono cen.easy: There are forty pages, and hundreds of names. "I never told anyone," says Siebe. "They would not believe me. And the people who would believe me were written in here."
Le pagine sono quaranta. I nomi sono cen.short: Forty pages, hundreds of names. "I told nobody. Those who would have believed me were written in here."

Siebe ti stringe la mano con le ultime f.easy: Siebe holds your hand with the last of his strength. His hand is warm and bony. He closes his eyes. He dies that night, in his sleep, with a normal temperature: Joost Maas measures it in the morning and writes it in the Register, underlined. You take the notebook to the estate and put it next to the Register. When you read them together, the names answer each other.
Siebe ti stringe la mano con le ultime f.short: Siebe grips your hand, warm, and dies that night at a normal temperature: Joost underlines it in the Register. You keep the notebook beside the Register. Read together, the names answer each other.

Siebe ti chiede di bruciarlo: non vuole.easy: Siebe asks you to burn it. He does not want "them" to find it after he dies. You burn it in the stove of the shed, page by page, in front of him. He watches the pages turn black and smiles. He is relieved. "Now they sleep in peace," he says. "All of them. And me too."
Siebe ti chiede di bruciarlo: non vuole.short: You burn it page by page before him, so "they" will not find it. Siebe smiles, relieved. "Now they sleep in peace. All of them. Me too."

Caro Willem, nostro padre sta morendo, s.easy: Dear Willem, our father is dying, if you still want to know. He is ninety, his mind is clear and his hands are warm: I check them every morning. Every evening he asks me to play something for him on the little organ in the house, and to play one wrong note, only one, so that he can hear it. On Sundays, in church, the choir sings perfectly. It makes me want to scream.
Caro Willem, nostro padre sta morendo, s.short: Dear Willem, our father is dying: ninety, clear-headed, warm hands. Each evening I play him one wrong note, so he can hear it. On Sundays the choir is perfect. I want to scream.

La famiglia della tenuta ha accettato la.easy: The family of the estate accepted the council's medal. I do not blame them: they are tired, like all of us.
